doors.history:
Brent's queer history goes back further than most people assume, but it's a general-borough record more than a Black-specific one — and nobody, including us, has yet put a name to a Black queer chapter of it.

A lesbian and gay social group has been meeting in the Harrow and Brent area continuously since 1971 — it started as the Harrow & Brent Lesbian & Gay Group, and still runs today as North West London LGBT, weekly, though its fixed home moved to Harrow long ago. Mosaic, the borough's LGBT youth project, ran in Brent until 2016, when austerity cuts forced it to close its doors here and relocate to Camden as an independent charity — its archive is now held at Willesden Green Library. In September 2022, that same library hosted 'Gaps in the Archive', a day inviting residents to hand over their own LGBTQ+ memories and memorabilia, as part of that year's Brent Biennial — an art festival across Kilburn, Willesden and Harlesden explicitly themed around queer homemaking as a form of resistance.

What's live now: Wembley Park Pride, the only Pride celebration the borough has, running its first full Pride Week in 2026 in partnership with West London Queer Project — and, that same year, Brent Council starting its first-ever attempt to map the borough's LGBTQ+ networks, working with LGBT HERO, because nobody yet has a clear picture of who's here or where they meet. None of that record names Black queer men specifically. This page is where that starts — if you're already meeting, tell us below, and we'll build the rest of this history around you rather than around a gap.

besideUs.name: Wembley Park Pride
besideUs.note: The only Pride celebration in the London Borough of Brent — run by the Wembley Park estate in partnership with West London Queer Project. 2026 was its first full Pride Week (28 June–5 July), building on years running as a sunset finale to London's Pride parade.

besideUs.name: West London Queer Project
besideUs.note: Community Interest Company connecting and supporting LGBTQ+ people across West London — co-delivers Wembley Park Pride's programme, including 2026's outdoor yoga session in the park.

besideUs.name: Brent Council's LGBTQ+ Inclusion Programme
besideUs.note: Launched in 2026 with the charity LGBT HERO — a borough-wide survey and the council's first attempt to map the LGBTQ+ networks already in Brent. If you're one of those networks, or want to be counted, this is the council actually asking.

besideUs.name: North West London LGBT
besideUs.note: Founded in 1971 as the Harrow & Brent Lesbian & Gay Group — still meeting weekly, every Tuesday from 8pm, now at The Trinity in Harrow, with members from across Brent, Barnet, Hillingdon, Hounslow and beyond. The oldest LGBTQ+ social group with Brent in its name.

besideUs.name: 100 Black Men of London
besideUs.note: Black-led mentoring charity running community mentoring programmes for Black children and young people — listed in Brent's own community directory.

worthTheJourney.name: Black Connection
worthTheJourney.note: UK-wide social network for Black queer men aged 50+, formed in 2020 and run out of London — regular meet-ups and an active, growing community.

worthTheJourney.name: African Rainbow Family
worthTheJourney.note: Registered charity by and for LGBTIQ+ people of African heritage and the Global Majority, founded 2014 — community, mental health, practical support and immigration advice, with a London base alongside centres in Manchester, Birmingham, Leeds and Swansea.

services.name: Sexual Health London (SHL)
services.note: Free, discreet home test kits and PrEP by post anywhere in London — order online, nothing to explain to anyone. Brent takes part in full, alongside Ealing and Harrow.

services.name: Patrick Clements Clinic — Central Middlesex Hospital
services.note: The borough's NHS sexual health clinic, on the Brent/Ealing border — walk-in and booked appointments, HIV and STI testing, PrEP.

services.name: 56 Dean Street
services.note: Soho's LGBTQ+ specialist sexual health and HIV service — Europe's largest, and long the home clinic of queer London.

services.name: Find your nearest NHS clinic
services.note: Every NHS sexual health service near you — testing, treatment, PrEP — searchable by postcode.

doors.quietNote: Checked 31 August 2026 — nothing organised specifically for Black queer men or Black LGBTQ+ people in Brent turned up in our own project records, the events and story archives, or a direct search. Brent Council is only now starting to map the borough's own queer networks (2026, with LGBT HERO) — which tells you this isn't a gap in our search, it's a gap the borough itself is trying to close. That's a report, not a silence. The door below is always open.

doors.history:
Camden's Black queer history goes back further than most boroughs get to claim, and BLKOUT's own chapter is only the most recent of several.

In the 1720s, on or near Tottenham Court Road, a probably-free Black man named Julius Caesar Taylor ran a molly house — arrested and convicted in 1728 for "keeping a disorderly House" and "sodomitical Practices." It's one of the earliest documented instances of a Black man in London organising queer space for others, three hundred years before this door.

Two centuries later, a different kind of gathering formed around Regent's Park Road. John Payne, an American singer who'd settled in London after the First World War, bought a home at number 17 that became, in his contemporaries' words, "the place to be" for the Black musical and theatrical community — Paul Robeson stayed there, Marian Anderson and Ethel Waters passed through, and it was there that Lawrence Brown first met Robeson and began the musical partnership that lasted the rest of their lives. Payne was also part of what his friends simply called "the group": a gay social circle of African and Caribbean intellectuals in 1930s and 40s London that included the composer Reginald Foresythe and — already the anchor of our Croydon and Lambeth doors — Ivor Cummings, the civil servant who later welcomed the Windrush generation at Tilbury Docks. A few streets away in Primrose Hill, one genealogical record places bandleader Ken "Snakehips" Johnson on Gloucester Avenue in 1939 — a year before the Belgravia flat, shared with his partner Gerald Hamilton, where he was killed in the Blitz (now on our Westminster door); thinner sourcing, but a Camden thread of its own. And for thirty-eight years from 1929, the Grenadian-British cabaret star Leslie "Hutch" Hutchinson lived at 31 Steele's Road in Belsize Park — an English Heritage blue plaque marks the house today.

Organising took a different, collective shape in the 1980s. The Camden Lesbian Centre and Black Lesbian Group — with the Black Lesbian Group operating autonomously within it — opened its own building at 54-56 Phoenix Road on 31 October 1987, the UK's first and only dedicated lesbian centre. It ran until funding collapsed in the early 1990s, and its archive now lives four hundred miles away at Glasgow Women's Library. This is women's history, not this door's core focus, but it belongs in Camden's record — and in 2024 it came back into the borough itself, when Camden People's Theatre's GRILLS went looking for it and held a Black LGBTQ+ link-up for the group's former and current members after the show.

A century after Taylor, decades after Cummings and Payne, we added our own chapter. In December 2019 we launched Black Men Who Brunch — "a brand new monthly event that will be shaped for us, by us" — with founding partners Shade Free (the UK's Black-owned LGBT+ events brand) and Arboretum, a members' club. It grew fast: a February 2020 sequel, a run of themed editions through 2020 and 2021, and by February 2022 an eighth edition billed "Future History." Brunch found its home at Old Diorama Arts Centre on Drummond Street, and at Regent's Place — the Euston Road business estate where British Land named BLKOUT an LGBT+ Community Partner, with Triton Café hosting our monthly gatherings. By June 2022's twelfth edition, "Welcomes the Summer Kitchen," the series had, in our own words, "built and strengthened friendships and connections, put the world to rights, challenged loneliness and isolation, learned new skills from filmmaking to knitting."

Alongside it, a second Camden tradition took root outdoors. Nzube Ufodike had nurtured a summer picnic in Regent's Park for several years before asking BLKOUT to co-host in 2022 as the BLKOUTside Summer Picnic — new partners Slay Storiez, The Black Experience and the Black Boy Joy Collective joined that year, and a 'best dressed' theme became a running joke worth dressing up for. The tradition has run every year since. In 2026 it became the BLKOUT Annual Picnic: Sunday 16 August, on the Camden side of Regent's Park near the zoo, an unproduced day built to flex from a usual ~65 to hundreds — bring your crew, bring your sound — closing with karaoke at Zodiac Bar and a community collection for LGBT+ Rights Ghana.

We haven't found a space currently run by and for Black queer men in the borough — the panel below is where that gets built. But the ground has already been walked. If you were at a Brunch, or you've been coming to the picnic since before we were involved, the panel further down is where you tell us, and the page changes.

besideUs.name: Old Diorama Arts Centre
besideUs.note: Euston's community arts hub on Drummond Street, where Black Men Who Brunch ran for years — today it hosts 50+ local groups rent-free, including the London Trans Choir and Yas Queen! Chess Club.

besideUs.name: London Trans Choir
besideUs.note: London's first trans choir, non-auditioned and open to all, rehearsing at Old Diorama Arts Centre.

besideUs.name: Yas Queen! Chess Club
besideUs.note: Women-led, LGBTQ+-friendly chess club at Old Diorama Arts Centre, open to all.

besideUs.name: Camden People's Theatre
besideUs.note: A studio theatre built around artists facing systemic barriers — 66% of its commissioned artists are LGBTQIA+, 47% Global Majority. Staged GRILLS (2024), the show that brought the Camden Lesbian Centre and Black Lesbian Group's history back into the borough.

besideUs.name: ZODIAC Bar & Club
besideUs.note: Trans-founded by Jade Phoenix Hoskins in 2020, at 119 Hampstead Road since 2021 — over £300,000 raised for LGBTQ+ causes, and where BLKOUT's own Annual Picnic closes with karaoke. Reopened May 2026 after a fight to stay open; an active petition backs it.

besideUs.name: The Black Cap
besideUs.note: Camden Town's legendary drag cabaret pub, the "Palladium of drag" from the mid-1960s — Paul O'Grady debuted Lily Savage here in 1978. Closed 2015, reopened March 2026 after a decade-long campaign.

besideUs.name: forum+
besideUs.note: The LGBTQ+ charity for Camden and Islington (formerly Camden LGBT Forum). It runs free wellbeing, social and cultural events, a hate-crime caseworker service, and curates the boroughs' LGBT History Month programme.

worthTheJourney.name: Black Beetle Health
worthTheJourney.note: The UK's only public health charity focused specifically on health inequalities for LGBTQ+ Black people and people of colour — resources, research and signposting, reachable from anywhere.

worthTheJourney.name: Melanin Vybz — London LGBTQ+ Community Centre
worthTheJourney.note: Bankside's community centre runs Melanin Vybz, a social space for Black and POC LGBTQ+ people — a short ride down the Northern line.

doors.history:
Croydon holds three generations of Black British cultural life in one family story. Samuel Coleridge-Taylor, the borough's internationally celebrated composer; his widow Jessie, who sought out a Whitgift schoolboy — a distant cousin through Sierra Leonean kinship networks — and claimed him into the family; and that boy, Ivor Cummings of Addiscombe, who grew up to be the openly gay civil servant welcoming the Windrush generation ashore at Tilbury in 1948. The name over every BLKOUT door belongs to a Croydon son, claimed by a Croydon family.

The line continues: David McAlmont, one of the great British voices, is Croydon's too. The Museum of Croydon's BlackOut exhibition keeps the borough's Black queer story on record, and BLKOUT's own heritage project, Ivor's Compass, is part of the borough's Coleridge-Taylor 150 year. This door is that story in the present tense.

here.name: Stanley Arts
here.note: South Norwood's arts centre, the borough's leading host of LGBTQ+ arts. Check their site for what's on.

besideUs.name: Croydon Area Gay Society (CAGS)
besideUs.note: One of the UK's longest-running LGBT social groups, meeting in Croydon since 1971.

besideUs.name: Croydon Pride
besideUs.note: The borough's grassroots Pride charity — back on Croydon ground at BoxPark in August 2026, with year-round work between festivals.

besideUs.name: Queer Croydon
besideUs.note: Croydon's LGBT+ community forum, carrying on where the old Croydon LGBT Forum left off: free wellness sessions, creative programmes and campaigning for LGBT+ adults across Croydon, with autumn 2026 events at Croydon Town Hall and local libraries.

besideUs.name: Museum of Croydon — BlackOut
besideUs.note: The borough's own museum has exhibited Black LGBTQ+ Croydon lives — including BLKOUT's story. The history is already on record here; this page is the living version.

worthTheJourney.name: Black, Queer & Thriving — Black Thrive Lambeth
worthTheJourney.note: Programmes and peer support for Black queer Lambeth — one stop up the line — including the Queer Minds peer group in Brixton.

worthTheJourney.name: Melanin Vybz — London LGBTQ+ Community Centre
worthTheJourney.note: Monthly group for LGBTQ+ Black people and people of colour over 50, at the Centre on Hopton Street, Southwark.

services.note: The borough's free NHS clinic — STI testing and treatment, contraception, PrEP — and free self-test kits posted to any Croydon address. 530 London Road, CR7 7YE. (Croydon runs its own service; the London-wide SHL scheme doesn't cover this borough.)

doors.history:
Enfield's Black queer history hasn't been written down — but it made history anyway. Phyll Opoku-Gyimah — Lady Phyll — grew up here, and the day in 1983 she was pulled into an Enfield Town shopfront while a National Front march passed became part of the story of why UK Black Pride exists. The borough with nothing built for Black queer men raised the woman who built it for all of us.

The rest — the elders of Edmonton and Ponders End, the nights, the photographs in shoeboxes — is still to be written, and the panel below is where it starts. First stories in, first names on it.

besideUs.name: Enfield LGBT Network
besideUs.note: The borough's LGBT+ consortium — voluntary and statutory organisations and residents working to improve life for LGBTQ+ Enfield.

worthTheJourney.note: Black-owned queer venue, now in Soho — straight down the Piccadilly line from the borough.

doors.history:
Hackney's Black queer history is recent by the written record, but it didn't start quiet.

Hackney Carnival had run for 23 years before a group of Queer, Trans, Intersex and Non-binary People of Colour — invited by the council's year-old Pride 365 programme to think about inclusion — built the carnival's first QTIPOC-curated space. Faggamuffin Bloc Party launched there in September 2018, described by its organisers as a reclaiming of carnival's own tradition of resistance through celebration, for and by queer people of colour. BLKOUT backed it from the start, and was there to dance.

That same year, Hackney Museum began working with us to collect the borough's QTIPOC oral histories — thirteen collected so far, ten local volunteers trained to gather more, and Bloolips drag performance artefacts added to the museum's own collection. That work continues, and it is still surfacing more of Hackney's story than any one page can hold.

here.name: Faggamuffin Bloc Party
here.note: QTIBPoC carnival collective born at Hackney Carnival in 2018, backed by BLKOUT from its first year. Believed to be the first sound system run by and for queer people of colour — still centring QTIBPoC lives at Carnival each year, with council cultural funding into 2025.

besideUs.name: Hackney Pride 365
besideUs.note: The council's year-round LGBTQIA+ programme, running since 2017 — history walks, drop-ins, film projects and club nights across the borough, not just one weekend in June. It's the programme Faggamuffin Bloc Party grew out of.

besideUs.name: Queertopia Consortium
besideUs.note: Community-led forum for Hackney's LGBTQIA+ residents — a sober community forum on the first Thursday of every month, plus brunches and markets through the year.

besideUs.name: City and Hackney LGBTQ+ Network
besideUs.note: Hosted by Hackney CVS, bringing together LGBTQ+ people, groups and services across the borough and the City to improve safety, services and rights.

doors.history:
Haringey's Black queer history isn't missing. It's foundational, and largely uncredited.

The Black Lesbian and Gay Centre was founded in 1985, and its northern base was an annex of Tottenham Town Hall on Somerset Road. The following year the borough opened the first council lesbian and gay unit in the country, run by Femi Otitoju. And on 2 May 1987 the Positive Images Campaign and Haringey Black Action marched three and a half thousand people from Duckett's Common to Bruce Castle Park under the banner Smash the Backlash — the first demonstration of its kind in Britain to put the lives of Black lesbians and gay men at its centre.

Section 28 became law in 1988, and Haringey was the borough it was written against. That is usually where the story gets told from — the losing end. But the borough was doing the thing first, and people who were there are still here. The rest of it — the rooms, the nights, the photographs in shoeboxes — is still being gathered, and the panel below is where it continues.

here.name: Wise Thoughts
here.note: Global Majority and LGBTQI+ arts charity, founded in Wood Green in 1999 and still running from the Creative Cultural Hub at Wood Green Central Library. Runs the gayWISE drop-in — housing and legal advice alongside the social — and GFEST, its cross-arts festival, every November since 2007.

besideUs.name: Bernie Grant Arts Centre
besideUs.note: Tottenham Green's home for Black creativity, named for the MP who opposed Section 28. BLKOUT screened here in 2017, during its James Baldwin season.

besideUs.name: Black Thrive Haringey
besideUs.note: The borough's arm of the Black Thrive movement, hosted by Mind in Haringey — peer-led research, cultural competency training, community assemblies and the Time2Heal app. Backed by ten years of Lottery funding. Where the borough's Black mental health work lives.

besideUs.name: Mind in Haringey
besideUs.note: Peer-led mental health support in the borough, including the Proud North London project for LGBTQ+ people, and the host of Black Thrive Haringey.

worthTheJourney.note: Peer-led sexual health and community building for queer men of colour, with outreach across north London. PrEP, harm reduction, and rooms that don't need you to explain yourself.

doors.history:
Islington's Black queer history is carried by people born here who took it out into the world, and by places in the borough that have kept making room.

Rev Jide Macaulay was born in Islington and grew up in Nigeria from the age of four. In 2006 he went back to Lagos to found House of Rainbow, a church that welcomed lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans and intersex people in a country hostile to all of them. When a newspaper reported on it in 2008 he had to leave Nigeria, and he built House of Rainbow into a global network from London. He was ordained into the Church of England in 2013. Twenty years after Lagos, the fellowship meets in person every month at Union Chapel on Compton Terrace, and on 6 September 2026 it premiered its anniversary documentary, Faithfully Me, there.

Lloyd Young was born in Islington too, to parents who came from Jamaica in the early 1950s. At 21 he opened his own menswear shop, Classique For Men, on Tottenham High Road. In the summer of 1994 he helped organise SHEGUN — A Day For Us, an open-air party in south London run by Black gay men and women. As he told us in 2021, for many people it was "a first Black Experience", and the name stuck for the project he went on to found.

Vernal Scott worked from inside the Town Hall. From 2003 he was Islington Council's Head of Equality and Diversity, and he went on to lead equality work at Oxford University and Leicestershire Police.

The borough's wider queer story begins in a park. On 27 November 1970, about 150 members of the newly formed Gay Liberation Front held a torchlight rally on Highbury Fields against police harassment. It was the first gay rights demonstration in Britain, and a plaque near Highbury Corner has marked it since 2000. In 2004, Camden and Islington Health Authority funded Sigma Research's study Ethnic minority gay men: Redefining community, restoring identity, in which men like us described community in our own words.

The stage has kept room for us. In November 2016 the King's Head Theatre on Upper Street revived Paul Boakye's Boy with Beer, a love story between two Black men first staged in 1992, in a production billed as its 25th anniversary. BLKOUT went to talk to the playwright. In spring 2022 the Almeida Theatre, just off Upper Street, gave Jeremy O. Harris's Daddy, the story of a young Black queer artist, its UK premiere. It held a Black Out performance for Black audiences on 12 April, and offered BLKOUT's community £10 tickets.

Today the threads run through ordinary places. The Melanated Queers Reading Collective meets monthly at Housmans on Caledonian Road. The London Archives in Clerkenwell holds Black African and Caribbean records worth asking for. On 25 October 2026, Melanin Vybz brings Black LGBTQI+ elders to Union Chapel for a Black History Month afternoon.

We haven't found a space currently run by and for Black queer men in the borough. If you grew up here, or you're making something here now, the panel below is where you tell us, and the page changes.

here.name: House of Rainbow
here.note: A faith community and global network centring Black, African and Caribbean LGBTIQ+ people, founded by Islington-born Rev Jide Macaulay. Its in-person service meets at Union Chapel, Compton Terrace, on the third Sunday of each month at 4pm, and it celebrated its twentieth anniversary there on 6 September 2026.

here.name: Black Meat Market
here.note: Erotic nightlife and private parties built for Black gay, bi and DL men. ROGUE comes to Bar Silver, 70 Upper Street, on Friday 23 October 2026. Adults only.

besideUs.name: London Friend
besideUs.note: One of the UK's oldest LGBT+ charities, at 86 Caledonian Road. Counselling, social groups, and Antidote, its LGBTQ+ drug and alcohol service.

besideUs.name: forum+
besideUs.note: The LGBT+ equality charity for Camden and Islington. It runs social groups and events, supports LGBT+ victims of hate crime, and puts together the boroughs' joint LGBT History Month programme.

besideUs.name: Melanated Queers Reading Collective at Housmans
besideUs.note: A free book club for queer people of the Global Majority, reading queer authors of colour. It meets on the first Wednesday of the month at Housmans, the radical bookshop at 5 Caledonian Road.

besideUs.name: Black Cultural Centre
besideUs.note: Islington Council's centre for residents of Black African and Caribbean heritage, at 16–18 Hornsey Road, N7, opened in November 2024. Community groups take it in turns to run programmes there: Black History Studies and the Sapphire Community Group ran the summer of 2026.

worthTheJourney.name: Melanin Vybz at the London LGBTQ+ Community Centre
worthTheJourney.note: A free monthly meet-up for Black and brown LGBTQ+ elders aged 50 and over, at the Bankside centre. On 25 October 2026 it comes to Islington for a Black History Month afternoon at Union Chapel: a short film, a panel, patties and rum punch.

worthTheJourney.name: Wise Thoughts
worthTheJourney.note: A Global Majority and LGBTQI+ arts charity next door in Haringey, running since 1999. It runs the gayWISE drop-in and GFEST, its cross-arts festival, and has an autumn and winter 2026 workshop programme.

doors.history:
When Ivor Cummings — the Croydon-raised, openly gay civil servant whose name is over every BLKOUT door — found the Windrush generation their first beds in the deep shelter under Clapham Common, the nearest labour exchange was on Coldharbour Lane. Brixton became Black London's front room because that's where the work was. And the room has always held us: beneath her Railton Road dress shop, Pearl Alcock ran the only gay bar in Brixton — a 1970s shebeen sheltering Black queer men from every borough — and ended her days a celebrated artist, hung at Tate Britain in 2005.

The record runs deep here: The Vox on Brighton Terrace, the first club of its kind run by and for Black queer people; the Brixtonian; Sistermatic's sound-system parties; Big Up's pioneering health work for Black gay and bisexual men — and Blackliners, the UK's first helpline and charity for Black people affected by HIV and AIDS. Arnold Gordon, who knew Ivor Cummings from Freetown to London, started it as a telephone line from his own spare room in 1988; within its first years the calls had outgrown the room and it moved into an office in Brixton. This door continues the story in the present tense.

here.name: Ajamu Studios
here.note: The Brixton studio of Dr Ajamu X — fine-art photographer, archivist and co-founder of the rukus! Black LGBTQ+ archive: three decades of celebrating Black queer men's bodies, desire and joy.

here.name: Black, Queer & Thriving — Black Thrive Lambeth
here.note: Programmes and peer support for Black queer Lambeth — including the Queer Minds peer group in Brixton.

besideUs.name: Lambeth Links
besideUs.note: The borough's LGBTQ+ signposting and community network.

besideUs.name: Black Men's Consortium — Mosaic Clubhouse
besideUs.note: Black men's mental health and community, Brixton.

besideUs.name: Brixton House

doors.history:
Lewisham's Black queer history is quieter in the public record than its numbers deserve — but it has already produced one of the country's most successful openly gay Black men.

MNEK — born Uzoechi Emenike in Lewisham in 1994, raised in Bellingham — has written and produced for Beyoncé, Madonna, Kylie Minogue, Dua Lipa, Stormzy and Little Mix among many others, and won the ASCAP Vanguard Award in 2016. He has spoken openly in interviews about being a gay Black man in an industry that doesn't always make that easy. He's not a BLKOUT story — he's Lewisham's own, and this page is proud to say so.

Beyond that, where the record exists, it's mostly ours to tell, and it mostly runs through one building. The Albany, Deptford's community arts centre, has hosted us more than once. In 2016, BLKOUT ran a series called E-troducing there. Over the years since, we've also supported a play staged at The Albany, and spoken at an event run by Black Gay Ink — Troy Fairclough's writing development scheme for Black gay men, which held workshops and showcases there into the mid-2020s before evolving into Black Rainbow Ink. And in April 2023, BLKOUT put out a direct call-out — #StrongerTogether — to Black bi, gay and/or trans men in Lewisham more widely: get together, get support from local professionals, decide what would work for you. 'Your crown has been bought and paid for.' We don't have a public record of what that group went on to do, which is exactly the kind of thing this page exists to find out.

What's real and building now: Deptford's Piehouse Co-op — a railway arch venue that closed and was fought back open by its community in November 2024 — and a council-backed capacity-building project launching in April 2026, explicitly prioritising Black and racially minoritised LGBTQ+ people as it rebuilds the borough's LGBT+ network. The infrastructure is arriving. If you were part of the 2023 group, on that stage, or in that writers' room — the panel below is where you tell us.

besideUs.note: Support for girls and LGBTQ+ young people (11–24) at risk of exclusion or exploitation, with a stated priority for Black, Asian and marginalised communities — part of the Lewisham Local capacity-building project launching April 2026.

doors.history:
Newham doesn't have a single named Black queer ancestral figure the way some of our other doors do — and we checked properly, including a lead into Claude McKay, the bisexual Jamaican-British poet who reported on London's docks for Sylvia Pankhurst's Workers' Dreadnought in 1919–20. His paper's office was on Roman Road in Bow, and the one sailor friend he names from those years was from Limehouse. Both are Tower Hamlets, across the border — not here. We're saying that plainly rather than forcing a fit.

What the borough does hold is a lost pub on Albert Road in the Royal Docks. The Kent Arms was, by the 1960s, a byword for dockers, sailors and gay Mods dancing together — remembered first-hand by Gay Liberation Front activist Stuart Feather. Jonny Woo's 2026 play Silvertown rebuilds it from interviews with the people who were actually there: dock workers, the women who lived alongside them, the African and Caribbean communities who worked the docks, and the LGBTQ+ people among them. Nobody has yet named a Black queer man who drank there. That doesn't mean there wasn't one.

Stratford has its own queer stage record too. Theatre Royal Stratford East staged Rikki Beadle-Blair's Bashment in 2005, tackling homophobia in the hip-hop scene, and his Summer In London in 2017 — the first full-scale show with an all-trans cast on a mainstream UK stage. Its cabaret night Queer Lates x Queerstory has run since at least 2020. And Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park itself carries a thread back to UK Black Pride's own origin story: Lady Phyll and the group Black Lesbians in the UK took a coach trip to Southend-on-Sea in 2004, which grew by 2005 into the first UK Black Pride — and the festival's flagship home is now the Olympic Park, paused for 2026 but due back in 2027. In August 2026, the Park hosted Queer Frequencies, a free weekend of Black queer music as part of V&A East's Music is Black festival, with Faggamuffin Bloc Party — the same QTIBPoC collective behind BLKOUT's own Hackney Carnival stage — running a full pre-carnival party at Sadler's Wells East.

BLKOUT's own history here is more recent, and it's ours outright. In February 2024, our co-director joined the panel for Newham Community Cinema's free screening of Little Richard: I Am Everything at Stratford Library, part of Newham's LGBT+ History Month — talking, on Newham's own ground, about one of the loudest, queerest Black icons American music ever produced.

Newham keeps a full LGBT+ History Month programme running every February, and Forest Gate Pride has run a free night at the Forest Tavern every month since it became a community interest company in 2021. It's real, and it's growing. What's missing is a room built specifically for Black queer men to walk into. That's the door we're opening.

doors.history:
Southwark's Black queer history runs deeper than almost any other borough's — most of it is only now being told.

Dr Cecil Belfield Clarke came to Britain from Barbados in 1914 on a scholarship to Cambridge, and in 1920 opened a GP surgery at 112 Newington Causeway, near Elephant and Castle. He served the borough there for 45 years, co-founded the League of Coloured Peoples in 1931, became Britain's only Black District Medical Officer by 1936, and later advised the newly independent government of Ghana. He was gay, and largely written out of the history he helped make — until a blue plaque went up on the site, now London South Bank University's Perry Library, in April 2023.

Berto Pasuka — the Jamaican-born dancer who co-founded Les Ballets Nègres, Britain's first Black-led dance company, and whom BLKOUT honoured with our own inaugural lecture at the National Portrait Gallery in 2019 — gave his home address as 35 Camberwell New Road in at least one contemporary document. This borough, not just a gallery in Westminster, is where he actually lived.

In 1992, the Black Lesbian and Gay Centre — founded in Haringey in 1985 — found its permanent home in a converted railway arch on Bellenden Road, Peckham: Europe's first purpose-built Black lesbian and gay centre, running until 2000. A Rainbow Plaque marks the site since February 2024.

And in November 2020, BLKOUT held our own Assembly there in spirit if not in person: a Sunday session with Southwark LGBT Network and Southwark Council, asking the borough directly — a Southwark Black queer hero, erased? It was about Dr Clarke.

The thread runs to the present. Carter the Bandit — a gay drill and rap artist of Ghanaian and Jamaican heritage, born and raised in Peckham — has built a career bringing queer energy into a genre that rarely makes room for it, praised along the way by Nicki Minaj and Saucy Santana. If you know more of this borough's story, or you were part of that 2020 Assembly, the panel below is where you tell us.

doors.history:
In 1920, a Jamaican poet was living on the Bow Road.

Claude McKay — later a defining voice of the Harlem Renaissance, and a bisexual man whose life his biographers have documented — spent 1919 and 1920 in London. Sylvia Pankhurst took him on at the Workers' Dreadnought, the radical weekly she published from Old Ford Road in Bow, in exchange for his room and board. He wrote from a little room on the top floor, covering a sawmill strike on the streets around the office and the docks beyond. When Scotland Yard raided the Dreadnought that year, McKay walked out past a detective with the article they were looking for folded into his sock, got rid of it, and went home to the Bow Road, where another detective was waiting. In a letter published that year he quotes what white men in Limehouse had been telling him about the summer to come. It is all in his own memoir, A Long Way from Home. He left for Harlem soon after, and the rest is literary history. Part of it was written here.

BLKOUT has its own history on this ground. In October 2018 we backed Gerrard Martin's B at Rich Mix on Bethnal Green Road, part of the And What? Queer Arts Festival: two Black men, Gerrard and Brandon, dancing together on a British stage, something programmers had kept off it for too long. Some of a capacity audience were moved to tears. With Monday-morning commutes looming, nobody wanted to go home after the post-show talk. In November 2022 we called a Black and LGBTQ session of the Black Voices on Policing consultation at 118 Bethnal Green Road, the same address where The Common Press now hosts Second Tuesday Monologues on Black Queer History.

Today, around 22,700 Black residents live in Tower Hamlets, among them Caribbean, Somali, Nigerian and Ghanaian communities. Black queer life is already happening here: Black Meat Market's nights at the White Swan in Limehouse, the Kreole Kiki Ball at Bethnal Green Working Men's Club, AfroYanga at Poplar Union. But the borough's own 2026 LGBTQ+ directory lists Bangladeshi, Muslim and Christian groups and no group that is Black-specific. That's the room this door is for.

doors.history:
Waltham Forest's queer history doesn't centre Black lives yet in the public record — but the borough has form as a place that gets there first.

In 2000, as part of the UK Gay Sports Festival, the borough hosted one of the earliest same-sex ballroom and Latin dance competitions anywhere — twenty years before Strictly Come Dancing recognised the same thing, according to veteran organiser Jacqueline Logan, who received a British Empire Medal for her thirty-year campaign in 2020. The same year, ELOP — running from Grove Road, Walthamstow since 1995 — organised the borough's first Pride, in Lloyd Park.

And in 2022, the William Morris Gallery gave Kehinde Wiley — the Black gay American artist who painted Barack Obama's official portrait — his first solo show in a UK museum: six large-scale portraits, of women he found on the streets of nearby Dalston. One of the most significant Black artists working today had his biggest UK museum moment in this borough's own gallery.

What we haven't found yet is a documented history of Black queer men specifically organising here — nothing playing the role Haringey's Black Lesbian and Gay Centre or Croydon's Ivor Cummings plays on those doors. That may be a real gap, or a gap in what's been written down. If you know different, the panel below is where the page changes.

besideUs.note: Running from Grove Road, Walthamstow since 1995 — counselling, mental health support and youth groups for London's LGBTQ+ community. Organised the borough's first Pride, in Lloyd Park, in 2000.

besideUs.note: The borough's own museum, in Lloyd Park — and the venue that gave Kehinde Wiley his first UK museum solo show in 2022. Worth knowing as a room that has already centred major Black work.

doors.history:
Westminster's Black queer history includes one of our own proudest nights — and it reaches back further than we knew, to a bandleader who died on a Westminster stage.

Ken 'Snakehips' Johnson, born in British Guiana, led the West Indian Orchestra — Britain's most popular Black swing band — through a nightly residency at the Café de Paris on Coventry Street, off Piccadilly Circus. He lived in Belgravia, at 91 Kinnerton Street, with his partner Gerald Hamilton. On the night of 8 March 1941, mid-performance, the club took a direct hit in the Blitz, and Johnson was killed along with members of his band. He had made a whole country dance to a Black, gay bandleader without most of them ever knowing his name for what it was.

Pride in London's parade runs through Westminster every year, past Trafalgar Square and Whitehall. Black queer organising has been inside that history for two decades: in 2005, 'Proud to B ME' brought Black and minority ethnic Pride communities together, with an after-party at the Pitcher and Piano on William IV Street, by Trafalgar Square. By 2008, the Black Gay Men's Advisory Group (BGMAG) — chaired by our founder Rob Berkeley — was negotiating directly with Pride London over funding for Black and BME floats and a dedicated BME stage.

On 15 February 2019, BLKOUT presented the inaugural Berto Pasuka Lecture at the National Portrait Gallery — sold out, part of LGBT History Month. Berto Pasuka, born Wilbert Passerley in Jamaica in 1911, moved to London and co-founded Les Ballets Nègres in 1946 with Richie Riley — Britain's first Black-led dance company. David McAlmont gave the lecture, 'Portrait of a Black Queer Briton', in five acts set to two centuries of music by Black composers. It was built as the first in a series, and it remains a genuine high point of our own record in this borough.

A year earlier, in April 2018, Let's Talk: Black Boy Joy ran downstairs at Ku Bar, Leicester Square, in association with BLKOUT and 56 Dean Street — an open-mic night by and for queer people of colour, with Marc Thompson among the speakers. Black queer London has moved through Soho in other ways too: our own archive carries a 2018 profile of Jay Jay Revlon, the ballroom scene builder behind English Breakfast and the House of Revlon, and a mention of a 2016 vogue battle held as a vigil in Soho Square. In 2025 the council's own archive started platforming Black queer artists through events like Black, Queer & Young.

Most recently: a Black-owned queer venue called COVEN, which started in Hackney Wick, opened its Soho headquarters — bar, café, community hub and five-floor club — at 30 Old Compton Street on 19 June 2026, on the former G-A-Y Bar site. Full details are in the directory below. If you were at the Gallery in 2019, in that room at Ku Bar in 2018, on a BME float, or you know a chapter we've missed, the panel further down is where you tell us.
